Indigenous women have been engaging with the UN for at least 50 years, at least. We've been here from the beginning. In 1977, when Indigenous peoples first gained direct access to the UN forum to speak for ourselves, Indigenous women, we were there. at the historic International NGO Conference of Discrimination Against Indigenous Populations in the Americas. Indigenous women went on to participate in the Working Group on Indigenous Populations, in the decades-long negotiations that produced the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, and in the advocacy that established and strengthened the three UN mechanisms dedicated specifically to Indigenous peoples. More recently, Indigenous women organized across regions through the consultations and advocacy that led to the adoption of CEDAW General Recommendation 39 on Indigenous women and girls. We have not simply participated in these mechanisms, we've helped shape them. Today, we engage across treaty bodies, UN agencies, special procedures and mechanisms throughout the UN system. Indigenous women are everywhere, and we've been here for generations. So the question of effective participation and effective Indigenous women's leadership is not simply about how we enter these spaces. It's about how we organize, how we bring other women with us, and how we sustain the institutions we built. We learned this early from our elders. In 1995, at the Fourth World Conference on Women in Beijing, Indigenous women from different regions found one another under a small canopy. And there, our elders made a commitment that we would never enter these international spaces alone. We would go home to build national, regional, and global Indigenous women's networks. I saw the importance of that years later at CEDAW. In my role as a senior Indigenous fellow with the Office of the High Commissioner, I was with Indigenous women from India who had just formed the National Indigenous Women's Organization. They had made it all the way to Geneva, but these national leaders were terrified to speak at the NGO meeting. I sat with them in a corner and pushed them. You came this far. You have to speak. Tell them what's happening to your women and girls in your community." And within that last five minutes of that meeting, they did. And among so many NGOs, they were selected to address the CEDAW committee directly. That experience taught me something, something important about indigenous women's leadership. Mentorship matters, but so does opportunity. Sometimes we need, sometimes what is needed is another Indigenous woman beside you saying, "You belong here. Go for it. Speak." But Indigenous women do not need others to give us our voice. When the opportunity is open, we know how to seize it, represent our communities, and make our voices heard. Effective leadership, then, is not always being the woman on the microphone. It's helping open the doors. It's mentoring another woman to walk through it and then watching her take the microphone for herself and her peoples. And for this, we also thank our indigenous leaders and key allies within the UN bodies, such as Miriam Masakisa, Chandra Roy, and Elsa Stamatopoulou, who held up the secretariat of the Permanent Forum for the last 25 years. And so another lesson came from law professor James Anaya when he was special rapporteur on the rights of Indigenous peoples. We asked him, "Why don't you specifically meet with Indigenous women during country visits?" That raised an important question about respecting Indigenous peoples' institutions while ensuring Indigenous women are heard. And it caused us to recognize something: We are Indigenous institutions. Indigenous women, we have been organizing for over 30 years. EKMIA, the continental network, is 30 years old, and FIMI is now 25 years old. But the Maori Women's Welfare League has organized Indigenous women for over 50 years. Our organizations are not outside Indigenous self-determination. They are only expressions of it. And look at what happens when those institutions are sustained. Indigenous women organize across regions and engaged CEDAW for years. That collective advocacy contributed to General Recommendation 39, a standard that recognizes both our individual rights and our collective rights. And that is effective leadership. We enter, we organize, We bring others, we build institutions, and we change law, policy, and systems. Thank you.

Thank you, Dr. Gonzalez, for sharing those experiences and reflections on what it takes to lead and to claim space within the buildings and the institutions that we are at at the moment here at the United Nations, and not least what it takes to keep leading. So with that, I would like to really thank all four panelists. What we have heard from Africa, from Asia, from North America, from the Americas more broadly, is a single powerful truth. Indigenous women have always led. Your leadership is what will carry this agenda forward. So thank you very much again. So I would like to, I think, invite the panelists to find your seats and hand back to the master of ceremony for a special moment, the presentation of FIMI's Indigenous Women's Leadership Awards. Thank you very much.

Thank you so much to all the panelists, and thank you, Bjorn, for leading us this important conversation. Now we come to a moment of celebration, a moment to recognize indigenous women's leadership, resilience, and the power of collective action. Those who know FIMI, I think, must be familiar with this. Since 2013, FIMI has been-- FIMI Indigenous Women's Leadership Award has recognized indigenous women's organizations whose work strengthens communities and creates opportunities for indigenous women and girls to thrive. This year, under the theme Sports for Indigenous Women's Wellbeing and Self-care, the award celebrates four remarkable organizations from four different regions, using sport as a pathway to wellbeing, empowerment, cultural connection, and community strength. We invite you to watch a short video recognizing this year's Indigenous Women's Leadership Award recipients. Is the video ready?

In every corner of the world, Indigenous women sustain life. With ancestral wisdom, collective leadership, and a profound vision for the future, they transform their communities every single day. This year, we celebrate indigenous women's organizations that make sport much more than a physical activity. They transform it into well-being, autonomy, leadership, the defense of rights, and hope for future generations. Since 2013, the FIMI Indigenous Women's Leadership Award has recognized those who, through commitment and collective action, are changing history from within their own territories. Because when an Indigenous woman leads, she strengthens her community, she inspires others, and she transforms the world. For our women and girls, football is a space to heal, to rebuild trust, and to strengthen community bonds after experiences of violence and conflict. Through traditional Kichwa games, AWA connects ancestral knowledge with self-care, mental health, and violence prevention, keeping memory alive across generations. In Assam, football is opening new possibilities for Adivasi girls, supporting their education and well-being, while helping them see themselves as leaders in their communities. In Fiji, field hockey is creating new spaces for girls and young women, not only as players, but as coaches, referees, and leaders. Four organizations, four territories, one shared vision, sport as a pathway to well-being, rights, leadership, and collective transformation.

Congratulations to this year's Indigenous Women's Leadership Award recipients, our Indigenous Women's Empowerment Kenya, Awak Ecuador, Purva Varati in Education Trust, Assam, India, and Aituki. we should be celebrating along with the work that Indigenous women are doing on the ground. Thank you so much. Now we move to the next segment, where we will be discussing from recognition, leadership to commitment. Our next segment from CSW70 to GR39 accountability that will connect to connect the commitments emerging from the 17th session of the Commission of the Status of Women with CEDAW General Recommendation number 39 on the rights of Indigenous women and girls. This is an opportunity for us to consider how international commitments can translate into practical actions, including through plural legal system, effective remedies, legal empowerment, Indigenous-led data and knowledge, dedicated resources, institutional accountability and meaningful follow-up mechanisms. To moderate this important dialogue, conversation, thank you so much, Bjorn. It's my pleasure to invite Ms. Leah Nicholas-McKenzie, Vice Chair of the UN Permanent Forum on the Indigenous Issues. The floor is yours.

It's a beautiful day. I would like to first acknowledge the traditional territories of the Lenape peoples. I am a proud member of the Walisagway Nation in Canada. And as one of the founding members of FIMI, this is really a full circle moment for me and for the organization. Now, this segment, as mentioned, looks at the issue of access to justice for all Indigenous women and girls from standard setting to implementation, which has long been a focus of the Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues. And I would like to take a moment to acknowledge my colleague on the forum, Amina Amhareth, and as well Miriam Masakisa from our secretariat. and pay tribute to Elsa Stamatopoulou, who's here with us today. She was the very first chief of our secretariat. Now, access to justice remains one of the most persistent barriers facing indigenous women and girls worldwide. Too often, they navigate legal systems that were not designed for them in mind. Systems that fail to recognize their collective rights, that overlook the intersection of gender-based and ethnic discrimination they face, and that leave the harms committed against them, including violence, dispossession of land, and violations of their cultural rights, unaddressed and unremediated. For many Indigenous women, justice also means the recognition of their own legal systems and ways of resolving disputes alongside and in dialogue with state justice mechanisms. Standards alone do not deliver justice, so this segment asks a harder question: What does it take to move from agreed language to lived reality? And to help answer that question, we are honored to welcome our panelists, who have each shaped this agenda from a different vantage point. I'd like to invite them to come join us. Her Excellency Beth Delaney is the Ambassador and Deputy Permanent Representative of Australia to the United Nations. Her Excellency Sandra Jensen Lande is the Deputy Permanent Representative of Denmark to the United Nations. Laetitia Boniface, who is with us online, was a member of the CEDAW Committee from 2021 to 2024 and was part of the group that prepared General Recommendation 39. Begonia Lasaga Baster is the Director of the Division for Gender Equality at UNESCO. And Adriana Quinones is chief of the Human Rights and Non-Discrimination Section at UN Women's Geneva office. Now, special rapporteur Albert Berume was meant to join us on this panel, but due to the delayed start, he had to leave. But we do acknowledge his commitment to both joining us on the panel and to his longstanding commitment to Indigenous women and girls. So first, I am pleased to invite Her Excellency, Ms. Beth Delaney. Deputy Permanent Representative of Australia, who has kindly agreed to open this segment and has agreed to stay a bit longer. I know that you have other commitments, so much appreciated. Excellency, Australia has its own ongoing journey with Indigenous rights and reconciliation domestically. How does that experience inform the position Australia brings to advancing GR39 internationally?

Thank you very much and good morning, everyone. It really is a privilege to join you here at the commemorative event of the first ever International Day of the World's Indigenous Women and Girls. Can I also express my condolences to our Nepalese family for the tragedy that's unfolding there. Can I also acknowledge the people whose land we meet on today, the Lenape people, as well as all Indigenous peoples who are joining us from around the globe, our Pacific, our family, and pay my respects to your countries and ancestors, elders past, present, and emerging. And can I acknowledge also the remarkable Indigenous women leaders joining us, your resilience, your leadership, cultural strength, continue to shape communities, nations, and international partnerships across the globe. So now to your question. So Australia's reconciliation journey is ongoing. It's taught us very important lessons about partnership, self-determination, and the value of Indigenous leadership. But our journey is far from finished. Indigenous women and girls in Australia continue to experience unacceptable rates of violence, overrepresentation in the justice systems, and persistent socioeconomic disadvantage. At the same time, in Australia, as in many countries, Indigenous communities, Indigenous women are leading solutions, strengthening culture, supporting families, advancing economic opportunities, and building more resilient futures. Under our national agreement on closing the gap, Australia seeks to embed shared decision-making and Indigenous-led approaches across government systems and services, and we don't really have time to go into examples, but I you to have a look at them. And that's because we know their leadership is not only vital for Indigenous communities, but also for addressing some of the most complex challenges facing our societies. And we also know that more sustainable outcomes are achieved when Indigenous peoples are partners in decision making, rather than the subjects of it. So Australia seeks to bring these same principles to our international engagement, including how we drive, I suppose, GR39, to recognise that Indigenous women and girls experience distinct and intersecting forms of discrimination, while also recognising the leadership, resilience and contributions they bring to their communities, societies and countries. We're working with Australia's First Nations people to bring their perspectives within Australia's foreign policy through our First Nations International Engagement Strategy. And guided by our international gender equality strategy, informed by our domestic experience, we advocate for approaches grounded in partnership, participation and self-determination. Australia believes progress is strongest when Indigenous women and girls are not only heard, but empowered to shape policies, programs and decisions that affect their lives. As we mark this first International Day of the World's Indigenous Women and Girls, it's time to move beyond recognition to action. Amidst growing global challenges and constrained resources, investing in the leadership, the knowledge, the agency of Indigenous women and girls is essential to building stronger, more inclusive and more resilient societies. And once again, it's a true honour to share this historic day, historic and hopeful, I think was one of the expressions, with you. And thank you again for allowing me to join.

Well, thank you, Excellency, and it is indeed a hopeful day. So we now turn to what GR39 demands of states in practice, and I misled you. Dr. Albert Barume is indeed with us. And so I am so pleased to welcome the Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. Mr. Special Rapporteur, from your mandate's perspective, what are the most urgent state obligations under GR39, particularly regarding access to justice within plural legal systems and free, prior, and informed consent, and where are states falling short today?

Thank you, Madam Chair, and I apologize for rushing you somehow. I was on my way to the airport. Let's just start by recognizing or joining those celebrating today, which is -- I absolutely do share the view it's a historical day. And the reason it is a historical day is actually part of my answer to your question. I do, as a UN Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Indigenous People, it is important to acknowledge the particularly disproportionate weight that Indigenous women and girls have been carrying for centuries, decades. and in contemporary times. And for that reason, I'm really, really pleased that the UN has decided to dedicate an international day to indigenous women and girls. In my report that I'm presenting to the Human Rights Council in Geneva this coming September on indigenous women reproductive rights, I do say something specific that I want to hear to repeat is that throughout history, wherever this has happened, every time indigenous peoples were first facing challenge, two major targets have always existed across regions. And those major targets have been indigenous peoples' land and indigenous women bodies. In that report, I highlight how it is critically important as we move towards celebrating the 20th anniversary of the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous People for states to acknowledge, recognize the importance of those two central issue to indigenous peoples. And I meant indigenous people, land and territory and indigenous women bodies. Those two through century decade have been and continue to be the two major target of policies, program seeking to annihilate or affect indigenous people's rights. So it's really an extraordinary day, and I'm very, very happy to -- that this day is actually finally seeing the light. My second point, Madam Chair, just to answer to your question, is that in the report that I'm presenting to the Human Rights Council in the coming September in Geneva, I'm actually underlining the centrality for state to institutionalize intercultural health policies, programs, and institutions. They are key to redressing those historical injustices. Because I think as the Excellency, the ambassador of Mexico did mention, it is important, a state cannot redress something it does not recognize first. then a state must repair if a state have to seek reconciliation. These are three key major steps. And it is important while state move to redressing, to acknowledging, to redressing and seeking reconciliation with indigenous women and girls, that those state put in place culturally sensitive health policies, programs and institutions that put at the center essentially two major things. First, the centrality of indigenous traditional knowledge, including midwifery, which was celebrated a few months ago. The traditional knowledge of indigenous people is and will continue to be central. Second, the free, prior and informed consent of indigenous women, including in the health sectors. Madam Chair, Again, once more, let me really thank you for inviting me to this very, very, very central and important event for redressing the historical injustices Indigenous people, and more specifically Indigenous women and girls, have gone through and continue to go through. Because, and that's my last point, my report do actually show how those historical injustices remain non-addressed and continue in different form in contemporary times. These are my point. Again, thank you, Madam Chair, for inviting me, and I do apologize for rushing you because I have to catch a flight. Thank you.

Thank you so much, Special Rapporteur, for that important perspective and also for your so important-- your report on Indigenous women and reproductive rights is just so important. So thank you again. So now let me turn to Her Excellency, Ms. Sandra Jensen Lande, Permanent Representative of Denmark. And my question, Excellency, Denmark has long positioned itself as a champion of gender equality on the international stage. How does that leadership translate into concrete support for the rights and priorities of Indigenous women and girls, both within Denmark's own realm and globally?

Thank you, Ms. Nicholas-Mackenzie. Thank you so much. And my sincere thanks to all the organizers today and to the Indigenous women and leaders in particular who are with us today, whether they're with us physically, online, or maybe spiritually. They have worked very hard to make this day a reality, and it is indeed a day worth marking. For the government of Denmark, gender equality, as you were saying, has in SRS HR and the rights of indigenous peoples are all key priorities, but at the same time, we have to acknowledge that our current advocacy follows very dark chapters of our history. For decades, beginning in the 1960s, women and girls in Kalaallit Nunaat, also known as Greenland, were subjected to contraception without full consent or adequate information, exactly the theme that the Special Rapporteur was just talking about. They experienced pain, humiliation, and systemic discrimination. most fundamentally, women and girls were denied the right to decide freely over their own bodies and their own future. In 2025, the Prime Minister of Denmark formally apologized for the injustice committed against Greenlandic women and girls. And the government of Denmark committed ourselves to working together with Nalaka Suizut, the government of Greenland, guided by truth, recognition, dialogue and reconciliation for a better future. But an apology must, of course, also be followed by action. That is why the Parliament in Denmark has recently adopted a compensation scheme for those affected, which will now be implemented. And Naalakkersuisut and the Government of Denmark are discussing how best to shed light on our shared history and to support reconciliation. We know that reconciliation requires listening, transparency, and sustained action, and we know that we still have a lot of work to do. The same principle guides our international engagement. Indigenous women and girls must not simply be the subjects of decisions. They must have a voice, a seat at the table, and the power to shape those decisions. This means ensuring that indigenous women and girls are able to participate meaningfully in the decisions that affect their lives, from climate action and the protection of lands, territories and resources, to sexual and reproductive health and rights. At the UN, Denmark therefore works for enhanced participation in indigenous peoples' representatives and representative institutions chosen according to their own procedures. We advocate for increased recognition of indigenous people's rights to self-determination and their distinct status as right holders, as well as the multiple and intersecting forms of discrimination faced by indigenous women and girls. And we support the human rights mechanism that hold us all accountable, such as the Universal Periodic Review and the special mandate holders. We just heard from one of them. We hope to continue working with all of you to shift these norms and standards. And we also translate our commitments into action through our development cooperation, through our partnership with the International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs, IWGIA, and the Inuit Circumpolar Council, Denmark supports Indigenous women's organizations across the world. Our partnerships include dedicated funding for Indigenous women and girls, ensuring that their own organizations have the resources to identify priorities and the change in their communities. So on this first International Day, let us celebrate the leadership of Indigenous women and girls who have fought very hard and continue to do so, and let us listen to them and support them. Thank you.

Thank you so much, Excellency, particularly for sharing the story of reproductive injustice suffered by Indigenous women in Greenland, as well as the actions that are being taken to address it. So we now turn to the normative foundations of General Recommendation No. 39 itself. And our next speaker is Ms. Laetitia Boniface, former member of the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women, joining us online. Ms. Bonifaz played a direct role in the committee's work developing General Recommendation No. 39. And so, Ms. Bonifaz, what does CEDAW General Recommendation No. 39 change for Indigenous women and girls that previous CEDAW jurisprudence did not address? And where were the key breakthroughs in its negotiation?

Thank you very much. I would have love to be with you in New York, but unfortunately, I have to join you online. I wanted to begin by expressing my sympathy to Nepal. My colleague, Vandana Nara, has been keeping us up to date with this tragedy, and my solidarity to everyone who's affected. diving into this topic, I'd like to say that General Recommendation 39 focused on and placed in the core the rights of indigenous women that hadn't been expressly taken into account in the original text that only talked about rural women. Indigenous women today in General Recommendation 39 have a new instrument which is serving to uphold rights not only within courts but also to understand the topic substantively, which is how to work on intersectionality and interculturality. Because All too often, it is thought that indigenous women only suffer discrimination because they are indigenous, or that they only suffer it outside indigenous territories. General recommendation 13.9, with the assistance of various organizations, including FIMI, which are with us today, managed to include in the articles of the general recommendation a reference to the expectation on all states relating to health, education, work, and everything involved in the relationship with the land. One of the fundamental issue was the interrelationship between indigenous peoples and not only women as individuals. Now, what is my stock taking of the General Recommendation 39? Well, fortunately, particularly UN Women has made it possible for us to have many fora in Latin America at least, where I've been involved, to ensure that general recommendation, the general recommendation is known about, because the first step has to be dissemination, raising awareness. I think that it is the first recommendation in the whole history of CEDAW that has been translated into seven or eight indigenous languages. This dissemination work needs to carry on, and it needs to be seen as a general recommendation that thinks about everyone, but it can also be tailored to a specific region, but also specifically to each country. We've been working in Guatemala, in Bolivia, Colombia, Peru, and in Mexico, my country, and We've been able to see how the acceptance of this and the fact that there was a new instrument was born out of the fact that people started thinking about cultural diversity, but particularly something that is fundamental, that is, for the first time in history, putting women, indigenous women and indigenous girls also in the heart of our discussions of all of these rights. Thank you very much.

Thank you so much, Ms. Bonifaz, for your work with Indigenous women to achieve GR39. And I am so delighted to hear that it's being translated into Indigenous languages. So now we turn to how the UN system itself is putting these commitments into practice. And I am pleased to welcome online Ms. Magonia Lasaga-Baster, Director of the Division for Gender Equality at UNESCO, who plays a leading role in indigenous language preservation and education. Ms. Lasaga-Baster, UNESCO's policy on engaging with indigenous peoples is aligned with the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. How is UNESCO translating this commitment into concrete support for indigenous women specifically particularly in safeguarding their role as knowledge holders and cultural transmitters.

Thank you very much, Chair. Good morning. It is a pleasure for me to begin this intervention in the language of my land, Basque. On behalf of UNESCO's Director General, Mr. Khaled El Enany, I'm extremely honored to join this first commemoration of the International Day of the World's Indigenous Women and Girls. I want to congratulate FIMI, UN Women, the Permanent Missions of Canada, Mexico, Ford Foundation, and so many friends that I have seen there, and so many people to have been able to achieve this International Day. And I think this day reminds us a very critical truth is Indigenous women are right holders, are leaders, and are agents of change. Across the world, they are the forefront of safeguarding languages, transmitting cultural practices, preserving knowledge systems, and strengthening community resilience. And yet, Indigenous women continue to face multiple and intersecting, as the last speaker has told us, forms of discrimination that limit their their visibility and their participation in decision-making processes. Recognizing and addressing these inequalities is essential both for advancing human rights and gender equality, but also for preserving the extraordinary diversity that enriches humanity as a whole. Across the field of competences in UNESCO, from education to culture, to science, from culture to communication and information, we seek to support indigenous peoples in safeguarding, transmitting and promoting their heritage, knowledge and languages, while ensuring that also in these issues, women are fully recognized and key actors and partners. And we are very proud as UNESCO to work with you. We are the lead agency for the Decade of Indigenous Languages, goes from 2022 to 2032. And we promote the preservation, rehabilitation, revitalization, transmission of Indigenous languages with all the Indigenous peoples. And recognizing that they, these Indigenous peoples, and particularly Indigenous women, are repository of identities, memories, traditional knowledge and worldviews. And you, indigenous women, are at the heart of these intergenerational transmission. We have worked with you, with some of you indigenous women, AI data scientists, to add your languages to Google's translation tool, like K'iche', Maya, Hunrik, and many other languages. We also work on the right to education in your own languages and grounded in your own cultures. And in climate resilience, we also work with many of you women, for instance, pastoralists in Africa, documenting the impacts of climate change and engaging you with you and always with you on things related to water conservation and protection of biodiversity. But let's be clear, this is not only about the past. You are contributing to contemporary cultural life as artists, storytellers, performance, craftswomen, writers and cultural entrepreneurs, renewing and reinterpreting the traditions for new generations. We are extremely happy to work with you to safeguard, create and share culture, ensuring that voices, knowledge and creativity continue to shape both the present and the future. And allow me to conclude with a very simple message. The preservation of indigenous languages, cultures, and knowledge systems cannot, and I repeat, cannot be achieved without Indigenous women. We remain fully committed to working, still working, continue working together with you, with Indigenous women, the Indigenous people, all member states, and all the United Nations system to advance to this objective. Thank you very much.

Thank you, Ms. Lezaga-Baster, for highlighting what implementation looks like in practice. And we only have a few minutes left, and thankfully we're at our final speaker in this segment, Ms. Adriana Quinones, Chief of the Human Rights and Non-Discrimination Section at UN Women. Ms. Quinones, how is the UN Women working to translate the CSW70 agreed conclusions and GR39 into concrete, accountable action, and what would be meaningful follow-up between now and CSW71? Ms. Quinones, we're not hearing you. I'm so sorry. It appears that we are having technical difficulties. With that, I think we're going to have to wrap up. for bringing this important conversation from commitments to international standards towards implementation, accountability, and action. So since we have very few less time to offer our closing reflection and call to action, I'm pleased to once again invite Teresa Javita.
Hi, I'm here. Can you hear me?
Yes, please go ahead.

Wonderful, thank you. And I'm so grateful that I could connect, just sending you a very warm hug from Geneva. You will see in the room, and you have in Geneva, our new team on human rights, rule of law, and on discrimination, which presents the most important opportunity that UN Women has created to link the commitments of the human rights treaty bodies, as much as we have with the CEDAW Committee on General Recommendation 39, to our work with civil society organizations, with other UN agencies, with governments, and to increase the accountability for access to justice as was set forth in CSW70. So we have put together a plan for the effective implementation of CEDAW General Recommendation 39 in partnership with FIMI and other indigenous women organizations. We will be reporting on implementation of CSW 70, and we had the privilege of counting with several indigenous women in the preparation of the expert group meeting, the Secretary General's report, and the agreed conclusions. We will continue to do the same from an integrated approach that brings the experience and the knowledge, and we hope to come back next year to report on this progress. It is an honor for UN Women to be joining this commemoration and we look forward to what comes. This is just the beginning. This is just the beginning of a dialogue of implementation and count on UN Women. Thank you.

Thank you for all of the statements. We're running over time. So two main conclusions and two messages to take away. First is the importance of partnerships, the importance of collective work. And in this context, before closing, I'd like to take some time to recognize the commitment of the state of Bolivia, which was behind the promotion of this global recognition, the International Day of Indigenous Women, obviously all of our friends, but also those in the Permanent Forum and the Secretariat. I'd like to thank them for making it possible to have this formal recognition today. I'd also like to underscore the importance once again of partnerships And on that point, I would like to invite all states, the philanthropic community to keep up these initiatives, these programs and maintain the same budget. Let's, we're continuing to advocate because We think that it is possible to continue investing in indigenous women's there as a political decision in the hands of many states, and we invite them to ensure that this day is an opportunity to reaffirm this commitment, but also turn it into programs, budgets, and funding. Finally, everyone's already said this, General Recommendation 39 from the CEDAW Committee is our tool. We have a global plan of action and indigenous women are very committed. We need to see the same commitment from our counterparts, states, the UN system, other associations and organizations and bodies that can join this recommendation and other important CEDAW recommendations. So, thank you very much to our panelists, to all of the guests here who came today, and those joining us online. And we invite you to ensure that this day that we're commemorating today extends throughout the rest of the year. Thank you very much.

So, as a reflection and call to action, so As we close this first commemoration of the International Day of Indigenous Women and Girls, let's carry forward not only recognition of Indigenous women leadership, but also our collective responsibility to act. We want to see actions, not only commitments. So today we have heard a very clear message that this recognition must lead to meaningful and equitable participation of Indigenous women and girls. Commitment must lead to implementation into actions. And And resources must be accompanied by accountability. So the leadership of indigenous women and girls is already transforming communities, protecting territories, biodiversity, sustaining culture. We have already heard from all the indigenous women panelists. So our responsibility is to ensure that systems and institutions around them create conditions for the leadership to follow. So on behalf of FIMI, UN Women, and our partner, the Permanent Mission of Mexico and Permanent Mission of Canada, we sincerely-- we extend our sincere appreciation to all the distinguished speakers, moderators, indigenous women leaders who are here joining us and also virtually, member states, UN entities, partners, and participants for making this historic first commemoration possible event. So thank you everyone and to everyone joining us through UNTV online. Thank you for being part of this important moment. So before we close, I would like to request the speakers, moderators and all Indigenous women delegates to join us for a group photo and our FIMI team will be guiding us to do that. So thank you everyone. Thank you for the patience and extending your time to be with us today. Thank you.
